competitors.description: The shipped ovos-core default intent pipeline, reduced to its intent-classifier stages in shipped order: Padatious high, Adapt high, m2v (Model2Vec) high, Padatious medium, Adapt medium.
competitors.notes: Purpose: what a user who changes nothing gets, as a baseline for every fusion. SOURCE: 'intents.pipeline' in ovos-config's shipped mycroft.conf: ["ovos-stop-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-converse-pipeline-plugin", "ovos-ocp-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-padatious-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-adapt-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-m2v-pipeline-high", "ovos-ocp-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-fallback-pipeline-plugin-high", "ovos-stop-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-padatious-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-adapt-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-fallback-pipeline-plugin-medium", "ovos-fallback-pipeline-plugin-low"]. SKIPS: the stop, converse, OCP and fallback stages need a running skill service, active-skill session state, OCP media skills or fallback skills, none of which exist in an intent-only benchmark. The Padatious and Adapt blocks repeat the shipped thresholds. The m2v block names the plugin's shipped default model, OpenVoiceOS/ovos-m2v-intents-multilingual, only so that the arena can pin its revision; the shipped config sets no m2v keys. A pinned snapshot loads the repo root, which the plugin documents as scoring the same as the int8 copy it loads by default. The model emits labels for 2,275 of the 2,380 ovos-intents-v5 test rows.

competitors.description: A softness-descending confidence mixer: Linha-Fina (trained statistical classifier) leads at high, Palavreado (order-independent keyword bag, no learning) backs it at medium, Nebulento (fuzzy string matching, the loosest/most tolerant of the three) closes at low.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Tests whether ordering engines by how loosely they match (trained classifier, keyword bag, fuzzy matcher) is a useful fusion axis. HYPOTHESIS: unlike trident (three-tier but engines picked for architectural distinctness), cascade-soft is picked for a deliberately monotonic 'strictness' gradient — trained classifier (least tolerant of paraphrase, most precise) -> rigid-but-vocab-flexible keyword bag -> fuzzy matcher (most tolerant of ASR noise/typos, least precise) — to test whether ordering engines by how loosely they match, not just by paradigm, is itself a useful axis distinct from trident's paradigm-diversity axis. Linha-Fina is a template-paradigm statistical classifier (see ENGINE_REGISTRY: 'linha_fina.opm:LinhaFinaPipeline', paradigm='template') distinct from both Jurebes (sklearn baseline family) and Padatious (neural+exact-gate), so this fighter and trident do not test the same top stage. exact_match not applicable to linha-fina/palavreado/nebulento (jurebes-only config key, verified absent from linha_fina/opm.py and palavreado/opm.py's self.config.get(...) call sites).

competitors.description: Four distinct paradigms, one engine each, staggered by tier: Padatious (neural template, exact matches included via its own internal padaos gate) leads, Adapt (keyword rules) backs it at high, then Palavreado (keyword bag) and Nebulento (fuzzy template) share medium recall, with Adapt low as the final catch-all.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Upper bound for one engine per paradigm: does maximal diversity keep helping past two engines. HYPOTHESIS: does a maximal-diversity cascade (one stage per paradigm, no paradigm repeated) beat curated 2-3 engine pairs? Slimmed from the original 7-stage config: dropped the explicit Padacioso-high stage because Padatious already runs padaos internally (disable_padaos=false) and returns conf=1.0 for perfect/regex matches before its neural score is even consulted, so a separate padacioso stage tested nothing padatious wasn't already doing; dropped the redundant padatious-medium retry since a second tier of the same trained classifier is not an independent paradigm and wasn't separately justified.

competitors.description: Two-stage variant of Linha Fina: intents are partitioned by skill_id, a top-level classifier maps the query to a single skill_id first, and only that skill's per-intent SVM engine resolves the intent. Same distribution and confidence gate as linha-fina-medium, registered under a separate opm.pipeline entry point (HierarchicalLinhaFinaPipeline in linha_fina/hierarchical_opm.py). Needs at least 2 domains and 3 intents globally before either stage can train (the plugin's own constraint).
competitors.notes: Same medium-confidence gate and thresholds as linha-fina-medium; 'domain_threshold': 0.0 keeps the top-level domain gate disabled (shipped default) so the comparison with linha-fina-medium isolates the two-stage routing shape. Hypothesis: domain-first gating should help precision on large multi-domain sets by rejecting cross-domain queries before any sub-engine scores, and be weaker or equal on small single-domain sets where the domain classifier has too little signal to train reliably. KNOWN BROKEN as of linha-fina 0.3.0a1: LinhaFinaPipeline.handle_initial_train (linha_fina/opm.py:138) calls self.containers[lang].train(), but HierarchicalLinhaFinaPipeline's containers are HierarchicalIntentEngine instances which have no .train() method (AttributeError on 'mycroft.ready') -- confirmed by a live train/match sanity run in this PR. Needs an upstream fix in linha-fina before this fighter can produce real predictions; kept in the registry so a fix is picked up automatically.

competitors.description: Trains one SVM per intent over one-hot keyword vectors, selecting the most relevant negative samples by fuzzy token-set ratio. Entities come from simplematch templates and wordlists.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; the per-plugin config pins the documented confidence thresholds. The engine itself is fixed: one SVM per intent over one-hot keyword vectors.

competitors.description: Tests whether zero-shot embedding matching plus fuzzy template slots can replace padatious with no training step at all: Model2Vec's prototype-mode pipeline takes the first shot with class prototypes embedded straight from registered templates, and Nebulento's fuzzy template matching backs it up for slot extraction and runtime-registered templates.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Training-free replacement candidate: zero-shot prototype matching plus Nebulento slots. HYPOTHESIS: m2v-prototype (see sibling fighter) shows that prototype-mode embedding similarity alone, with no trained head, can match runtime-registered intents. But it still lacks slot extraction. Nebulento fills that gap with template-based slot extraction and its own runtime-registered templates, so pairing it with the prototype pipeline's zero-shot front door tests a fully training-step-free replacement for padatious, not merely a front door for it. Comparators: padatious-medium (the trained baseline this fighter is trying to unseat) and m2v-prototype (isolates whether adding Nebulento's fuzzy backstop helps over the pure prototype fighter alone). conf_high/conf_medium/conf_low on the prototype block are the cosine-calibrated defaults from ovos-m2v-pipeline PR #91. REQUIRES ovos-m2v-pipeline>=0.9.0a1 — the calibrated thresholds land with ovos-m2v-pipeline#91; sweeps run before that PR merges and releases exercise the pipeline's code defaults instead, so this fighter's sweep must be sequenced after #91 merges. There is no plugin floor/pin field in this registry schema, so the floor must already be installed in the runner environment.

competitors.description: Trains one word-level Markov chain per intent from example utterances and picks the intent whose chain yields the lowest perplexity; confidence is derived from perplexity. Trains in milliseconds with no GPU.
competitors.model: order-2 word-level Markov chains, Kneser-Ney smoothing with backoff
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; the per-plugin config pins the documented model parameters (n-gram order, smoothing, backoff, stemming, char fallback) and confidence thresholds.

competitors.description: The historical Mycroft-AI intent order, before OVOS restructured the pipeline into confidence-interleaved stages: Adapt is the primary keyword-rule parser, Padatious runs only as a fallback after Adapt fails to match anything.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Reproduces the historical Mycroft ordering (Adapt first, Padatious as fallback) as a baseline. SOURCE: mycroft-core PR #939 ('Implement Padatious support (examples based intent parser)', MatthewScholefield) added Padatious to mycroft-core by making PadatiousService inherit from FallbackSkill (per forslund's review comment 'Make PadatiousService inherit from FallbackSkill to fix new fallback changes' on that PR) — i.e. Padatious was wired in as a fallback handler invoked only when Adapt's IntentBuilder grammar produced no match, not as a co-equal parallel matcher. Author confirmed back-compat ('Adapt will still work :)'). This is the inverse of the modern OVOS/mycroft-dev order (see ovos-stock.json and current MycroftAI/mycroft-core dev intent_service.py, which interleaves padatious-high ahead of adapt) — the point of this fighter is to test whether that later re-ordering (template-first) actually helped, by running the original adapt-first/padatious-fallback shape through the arena. Modeled as adapt-high -> padatious-medium: Adapt gets first shot at its own high gate; Padatious's medium tier (not high) reflects that classic Padatious ran as a general-purpose fallback rather than a first-look high-confidence matcher. Arena skips: fallback-skill priority tiers (90-99 catch-all range documented in Mycroft's Fallback Skill docs) don't exist as an arena stage — Padatious substitutes directly for 'the fallback', consistent with the historical mechanism. It is also the reference for an Adapt-front stage: nebulapt asks the same question with Nebulento behind Adapt.

competitors.description: Padacioso's deterministic, regex-based template matcher takes the first shot and extracts slots from an exact match; Nebulento's fuzzy string matching mops up anything the strict templates miss. Both engines are training-free and dependency-light, making this the lightweight padatious replacement candidate for installs where model2vec is not available.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Training-free pair: exact Padacioso templates with a fuzzy Nebulento fallback. HYPOTHESIS: Padacioso's high-confidence exact template gate plus Nebulento's fuzzy fallback should catch both exact and near-miss phrasings without any training step, unlike padatious or m2v-based fighters which need a trained model. Nebulento runs at its own low-confidence gate (conf_low) rather than medium so it actually fires as a fallback instead of sitting nearly silent behind Padacioso's high gate; conf_high/conf_med/conf_low values are copied verbatim from the single-engine nebulento-medium template fighter, only the pipeline tier differs.

competitors.description: Nebulento × Adapt fusion — precise keyword rules take the first shot, fuzzy matching mops up typos and ASR noise, and Adapt medium catches the remainder.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Keyword-side precision/recall test: strict Adapt backed by fuzzy Nebulento. HYPOTHESIS: does a strict keyword-rule engine (Adapt, low false-positive but brittle to phrasing/typos) at high confidence, backstopped by a fuzzy keyword matcher (Nebulento, tolerant of ASR noise and near-misses) at medium, and a lower-bar Adapt retry, beat either engine alone? Adapt and Nebulento are different matching strategies (strict rule vs fuzzy), so this tests real precision/recall complementarity, not a duplicate.

competitors.description: Padatious × Nebulento fusion — the neural parser leads at high confidence, fuzzy string matching mops up typos and ASR noise, neural medium catches the rest.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Template-side test of neural Padatious against fuzzy Nebulento on paraphrase and noise. HYPOTHESIS: does a neural template classifier (Padatious) at high confidence, backed by a fuzzy template matcher (Nebulento) tuned for typos/ASR noise, beat either alone — and does retrying Padatious at a looser gate afterward recover cases the fuzzy stage still missed? Padatious's internal padaos exact-match gate already covers regex-perfect input (verified in ovos_padatious/intent_container.py), so this pair specifically probes the neural-vs-fuzzy paraphrase gap, not exact-match duplication.

competitors.description: Fuzzy-matching intent engine: compares utterances against example sentences with string-similarity ratios instead of exact rules, trading precision for resilience to typos and ASR noise.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; per-plugin config keeps the shipped defaults.

competitors.description: Deterministic, regex-based drop-in replacement for Padatious. No training step and no false positives on unseen phrasings — what you template is exactly what you match.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; per-plugin config keeps the shipped defaults.

competitors.description: Same Padatious engine as padatious-medium, with the plugin's own two-stage DomainIntentContainer switched on via 'domain_engine': true: utterances first route to a skill_id-scoped domain container, then match against that domain's intents only.
competitors.notes: Same plugin id and medium-confidence gate as padatious-medium; the only config change is flipping 'domain_engine' from false to true, which swaps the internal IntentContainer for DomainIntentContainer (ovos_padatious/domain_container.py). Hypothesis: domain-first two-stage routing should help precision on large multi-domain intent sets (fewer cross-domain false positives) at the cost of an extra routing step, and be roughly neutral-to-worse on small single-domain sets where there is no domain structure to exploit.

competitors.description: Lightweight neural intent parser trained on expanded example sentences. The OVOS default intent engine: fast to train, fast to match, tolerant to small variations in phrasing.
competitors.notes: Single-stage pipeline at the plugin's own medium-confidence gate; per-plugin config keeps the shipped defaults.

competitors.description: Same Padatious engine as padatious-medium, with the plugin's own exact-match regex layer switched off via 'disable_padaos': true: every utterance goes straight to the FastText-similarity IntentContainer match, skipping the padaos regex pre-pass.
competitors.notes: Same plugin id and medium-confidence gate as padatious-medium; the only config change is flipping 'disable_padaos' from false to true. padaos is the exact-match regex layer inside padatious (IntentContainer(disable_padaos=...)); this fighter exists to quantify how much accuracy it actually buys, particularly on exact-template-match utterances, versus the training/boot-time cost of maintaining it. Padatious itself is not changing: disable_padaos stays a permanent, opt-in option in the plugin regardless of what these numbers show.

competitors.description: A three-tier confidence mixer across three genuinely distinct template paradigms: Padatious (learned template similarity + internal exact-match gate) at high, Jurebes (sklearn MLP classifier over TF-IDF features, the top-accuracy baseline on the intents-for-eval en-US template board) at medium, Nebulento (fuzzy string matching) as the loosest low-confidence catch-all.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Three distinct paradigms across the high/medium/low ladder: does a full confidence cascade beat any two-engine fusion. HYPOTHESIS: does mixing three architecturally distinct classifiers by descending confidence tier — neural-template-with-exact-gate (Padatious) high, statistical-ML classifier (Jurebes) medium, fuzzy-string (Nebulento) low — beat any two-engine fusion in the league? Unlike frankenparse (which mixes paradigms but stays single-tier-per-engine at similar confidence bands), trident deliberately spans the full high/medium/low ladder with one engine per rung, so it also probes whether a strict confidence-descending cascade (not just paradigm diversity) is itself a useful shape. BASELINE SELECTION: 'mlp_shallow' is the top-accuracy entry on frontend-static/public/data/benchmark-intent_template-intents-for-eval-en-US.json among all jurebes-* competitor_ids (accuracy 0.8154, beating jurebes-sgd-modified-huber at 0.8143 and every other of the ~55 published jurebes sklearn baselines on that board). Config key verified in jurebes/opm.py (self.baseline = self.config.get('baseline', 'linear_svc')) and jurebes/baselines.py ('mlp_shallow': lambda: _p(tfidf_word(), MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64,), max_iter=500))). exact_match set to false per spec (jurebes/opm.py: self.exact_match = bool(self.config.get('exact_match', True)) — forced off here so this fighter tests the trained MLP classifier itself, not jurebes's own internal exact-template short-circuit, which would otherwise duplicate what Padatious's high-tier stage already does one step earlier in the cascade).

competitors.description: A pure zero-shot fighter: Model2Vec's prototype-mode pipeline embeds each intent's templates into a class prototype at registration time and matches utterances against those prototypes by cosine similarity, with no trained classification head at all.
competitors.notes: HYPOTHESIS: every other intent fighter ultimately relies on a classifier (Padatious, Nebulento, or Model2Vec's own trained label set) that must see an intent's templates at a training step before it can match against them. Prototype mode instead embeds a class prototype directly from the templates handed to it at registration, so intents registered at runtime — after the pipeline is already live, with no retrain — are immediately matchable. This isolates the open-world/zero-shot axis: can embedding-prototype similarity alone, with no trained head, replace a trained classifier's raw matching accuracy. conf_high/conf_medium/conf_low are the cosine-calibrated defaults from ovos-m2v-pipeline PR #91, not the classifier-mode thresholds of the m2v-v5 heads. REQUIRES ovos-m2v-pipeline>=0.9.0a1 — the calibrated thresholds land with ovos-m2v-pipeline#91; sweeps run before that PR merges and releases exercise the pipeline's code defaults instead, so this fighter's sweep must be sequenced after #91 merges. There is no plugin floor/pin field in this registry schema, so the floor must already be installed in the runner environment.

competitors.notes: Voice-variant fighter complementing espeakng-m1: same engine and language, female variant appended to the language code (en-us+f1). Requires the espeak-ng binary on the system.

competitors.description: Wraps the espeak-ng command-line synthesizer, a compact formant-synthesis engine covering over 100 languages and accents. This fighter runs the m1 male voice variant on US English.
competitors.notes: README reference configuration; requires the espeak-ng binary on the system. The voice variant is appended to the language code (en-us+m1).

competitors.description: The Google Translate read-aloud voice via the gTTS library; no account required. The British English accent is selected with the co.uk top-level domain.
competitors.notes: Same plugin as google-tx-en-us under a different tld — a distinct competitor (US vs UK accent).

competitors.description: Synthesizes through the undocumented Google Translate speech endpoint via gTTS, pinned to the US English accent via the tld option.
competitors.notes: lang/tld pair from the plugin's documented REGIONAL_CONFIGS map for en-US. The README warns this endpoint is unofficial and unsuitable for production or commercial use.

competitors.description: Client for a MaryTTS server (or MaryTTS-compatible APIs such as OpenTTS and Larynx); the server synthesizes with hidden semi-Markov model and unit-selection voices.
competitors.notes: Requires a separately hosted MaryTTS server; README reference configuration.

competitors.description: Wraps the Mimic 1 binary, a flite-based concatenative synthesizer; voices are festvox flitevox files loadable from paths or URLs.
competitors.notes: Requires the mimic binary; README reference configuration with the ap voice.

competitors.description: Zero-shot multilingual (600+ language) TTS from the k2-fsa/sherpa/icefall team, run locally via the omnivoice/torch runtime. Supports voice cloning (ref_audio), free-text voice design (instruct), or letting the model pick a speaker automatically ('auto', used here). Arabic is first-class, with 22 regional varieties as distinct lang tags.
competitors.notes: Runs a local multi-GB model (CPU or CUDA, auto-detected); no API key or remote server required, unlike the Azure/Google cloud TTS fighters. GPU strongly recommended for real-time synthesis; 'lazy' loading is the plugin default so config-only validation does not require the weights.

competitors.description: The classic energy/denoise VAD extracted from the old ovos-listener: speech is a frame whose debiased RMS energy reaches a fixed threshold. No model, CPU-only.
competitors.notes: Runs the plugin's threshold method. The shipped all method compares each frame with the loudest frame since reset(); the bench resets the engine before every clip, so under that method the first frame of every clip is speech.

competitors.description: Silero neural voice-activity detector running on a small ONNX model; the listener's default VAD. Robust to music and environmental noise.
competitors.notes: Single VAD fighter at the plugin's own threshold; speech decision is 'any voiced frame in the clip'.

competitors.description: The classic WebRTC energy/GMM voice-activity detector. Tiny, CPU-only and fast; aggressiveness 0-3 trades false-accepts against false-rejects (3 = most aggressive at rejecting non-speech).
competitors.notes: Single VAD fighter; vad_mode pins the aggressiveness. A different vad_mode is a different competitor.

competitors.description: openWakeWord 'hey mycroft' fronted by a Silero pre-wake VAD gate: the detector only runs on clips the VAD calls speech, suppressing false-accepts on music and noise at the risk of missing very quiet speech.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Measures whether a pre-wake Silero VAD gate cuts false accepts on non-speech versus the bare detector. Combo fighter: wake-word engine + pre-wake VAD. The same engine without the VAD, or with a different VAD, is a different competitor.

competitors.display_name: openWakeWord + Silero VAD + speaker verifier (hey mycroft)
competitors.description: The full listener stack for 'hey mycroft': a Silero pre-wake VAD gate, then openWakeWord, then a speaker-verification confirm. Both gates push the false-accept rate down; the benchmark shows the false-reject cost.
competitors.notes: Purpose: The full listener stack (VAD gate plus speaker verifier) as the reference for the openWakeWord stack family. Combo fighter: pre-wake VAD + wake-word engine + verifier. Each distinct (engine, VAD, verifier) triple is its own competitor.

competitors.description: openWakeWord 'hey mycroft' followed by a speaker-verification gate: an activation only counts when the verifier confirms it, trading a small false-reject increase for fewer false-accepts.
competitors.notes: Purpose: Measures whether a speaker-verification gate cuts false accepts versus the bare detector. Combo fighter: wake-word engine + verifier. The same engine without the verifier is a different competitor.
